prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val2] SLA tiers (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Tier" · longest unbreakable word 84px · one-line width 105px
  col 2: header "Monthly uptime commitment" · longest unbreakable word 91px · one-line width 207px
  col 3: header "Service credit" · longest unbreakable word 54px · one-line width 100px
  col 4: header "Support channels" · longest unbreakable word 77px · one-line width 531px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare SLA tiers by uptime commitment, service credit, and available support.","reading":"Readers scan tier names down the first column, compare commitments and credits across rows, then read support details within each tier. Longer support descriptions will set row heights, giving headers and other cells room to wrap where needed.","groups":["Monthly uptime commitment and service credit are comparable numeric terms; their values should be easy to scan down their columns.","Tier identifies each row, while support channels describe the service available for that tier."],"keep_intact":["Tier names, including Mission-critical","Uptime percentages and service credit percentages","Individual words and identifiers"],"may_wrap":["Monthly uptime commitment and Service credit headers at word boundaries","Support channel descriptions at word boundaries"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[126,170,112,311],"idea":"Balance clear tier labels and numeric columns with substantial space for support descriptions, allowing the uptime header to wrap."},{"name":"B","widths":[110,228,100,281],"idea":"Keep the uptime header on one line and give the numeric terms a prominent comparison area, accepting more wrapping in support descriptions."},{"name":"C","widths":[125,145,95,354],"idea":"Give support descriptions the most space while using compact numeric columns and allowing both numeric headers to wrap."}]}
